description:
FIRE-X komandası olaraq kosmosda yanğın təhlükəsizliyinə qarşı NASA dataları, ESP32 aparat təminatı və AI (RAG) texnologiyasını birləşdirən real məhsul qururuq!

Biz: IoT və AI sahəsində təcrübəli komandayıq.

Niyə biz: Real cihazla işləyən, 1-ci yeri hədəfləyən güclü layihə.

Axtardığımız: Frontend və ya təqdimata dəstək verə biləcək bacarıqlı üzvlər. Qoşul, qalib komandanın bir hissəsi ol!
summary: FIRE-X turns NASA's microgravity combustion experiments into fire-safety answers for spacecraft and future lunar and Martian habitats. We built a bilingual (English/Azerbaijani) web platform on 407 rows from official NASA PSI tables (FLEX, BASS-II, SAFFIRE-I): a data explorer, analytics on oxygen, airflow and extinction, a mission simulator that gives a fire hazard index for the ISS, Orion, a lunar base, a Mars base, a rover and an EVA suit, and an AI assistant that answers only from the database and cites experiment IDs. We also built a working ESP32 sensor node (smoke, methane and IR flame sensors with a siren) in a 3D-printed enclosure, streaming live data to the dashboard. In orbit, flames are slower, cooler and harder to detect, and partial-gravity data barely exist yet. FIRE-X makes the existing evidence usable for mission designers and shows the same detection logic on real hardware.
details:
What it does

- Data Explorer: filter 569 records by investigation, fuel, outcome, oxygen level and data source; compare records and export CSV with a provenance column.

- Analytics Hub: extinction diameter vs oxygen (FLEX), burn time vs airflow (BASS-II), material comparisons and outcome frequencies.

- Mission Simulator: a Fire Hazard Index (1-10) and ranked relevant NASA investigations for the ISS, Orion, a lunar base, a Mars base, a pressurized rover, an EVA suit or a custom atmosphere. The index is a transparent heuristic based on oxygen fraction, pressure, material and gravity: a screening and teaching tool, not a certified model.

- AI Research Assistant: answers questions using live SQL queries over the database and cites experiment IDs. It labels verified and illustrative records and is instructed not to invent data.

- Hardware Node: ESP32 with MQ-2 smoke, MQ-4 methane and IR flame sensors and a buzzer siren; auto-baseline gas detection with heater warm-up and an alarm latch; a 3D-printed enclosure; a live dashboard that polls the board over Wi-Fi.

Key insights

1. Higher oxygen lets droplet flames survive to smaller diameters, so oxygen-enriched cabins and suits need more safety margin.

2. BASS-II shows a flammability corridor: very low airflow starves the flame, high airflow blows it off, and gentle cabin-like ventilation is the most dangerous band.

3. FLEX "cool flames" burn at temperatures ordinary heat detectors may miss, which supports gas and smoke sensing.

4. Partial gravity is still a data gap (LUCI and FM2 are future experiments), so lunar and Martian estimates are shown as uncertain.

Data honesty

407 records are row-level exports of official NASA PSI tables. 162 additional records were compiled by the team from NASA publications to cover investigations with no public table; they are labelled "illustrative" in the API, explorer, CSV export and AI answers, and are never presented as measurements.

Benefits and impact

Mission designers, students and safety engineers can explore real flight data in minutes instead of reading dozens of reports. On Earth, the sensor node demonstrates low-cost gas and flame detection for homes, vehicles and industry.

Creativity

FIRE-X connects open flight data, an AI assistant that cites its sources and a physical detector into one system.

Tools

Python, FastAPI, SQLite, JavaScript, Three.js, Chart.js, OpenAI API (gpt-4o-mini), ESP32 / Arduino, MQ-2, MQ-4 and IR flame sensors, 3D printing, GitHub Actions, Render.

Team SpaceAz (Ganja, Azerbaijan)

Murad Fatullazada (lead, hardware), Raiz Hakimov (frontend, 3D), Şahvaled Valizade (security, AI guardrails), Huseyn Alirzayev (data science). Team mentor: Omar Abdullayev. He mentored our team throughout the project and helped us a lot. As a member of the local organizing team, he stepped back from the final round and from judging, in line with the event rules.
